scenes.headline: How a language model runs on three-valued weights
scenes.sub: Ternary15M: every linear layer is −1, 0 or +1.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Dune! Ternary15M is a tiny story-writing model where every linear weight is minus one, zero, or plus one. Here's how that works.

scenes.text: Every weight is a sign, so a dot product becomes adds, subtracts and skips.
scenes.say: The idea: train it ternary from the start. Each weight is just a sign, so a dot product becomes adds, subtracts and skips, plus one scale.

left.title: Float weights
left.say: With float weights, every term in a dot product is a hardware multiply, and multiplies are the expensive part.

right.title: Ternary weights
right.say: With ternary weights, plus one adds the input, minus one subtracts it, and zero skips it. One scale multiply per output channel remains.

scenes.title: Training on signs
scenes.say: Rounding has no gradient, so you can't train signs directly. Quantization-aware training gets around that.

items.say: Keep a full-precision latent copy of every weight.
Divide each row by its mean absolute weight. That decides which weights round to plus or minus one, and which to zero.
Round, and run the forward pass on those ternary weights.
On the way back, pretend the rounding wasn't there, and update the latents.

scenes.label: the shipped ternary model, down from a 182 MB latent checkpoint
scenes.note: the FP32 embedding table is about 37 MB of it
scenes.say: The export is forty-three megabytes. But most of that is the full-precision embedding table. At this scale, the vocabulary, not the matmuls, dominates.

scenes.label: validation loss for hard ternary over the latent model
scenes.note: 1.61 vs 1.60 on TinyStories; one self-reported run
scenes.say: And going fully ternary costs about a hundredth of validation loss, on one self-reported run that cost about seventy cents.

scenes.text: Train in the quantization you ship: signs plus one scale per channel.
scenes.mark: Train in the quantization you ship
scenes.say: Train in the quantization you ship: signs plus one scale per channel, at almost no cost in loss.
To recap: signs instead of floats, adds instead of multiplies, and a straight-through estimator to train it.
